title: On Top Of The World: How a Group of Norwegian School Friends Created One of Europe’s Finest Boutique Festivals
summary: Presented in Luster, Western Norway, on an epic fjord, Bergtatt is one of Europe’s most specular and remote festivals, with a carefully-curated lineup. It's a big-hearted fest that does things differently.
contentText:
Norway is on top, in just about every meaningful way. Its 5.6 million population is blessed with an enviable standard of living, world-beating Winter Olympians, your new favorite soccer player , and a crop of standout recording artists, from electronic DJs and producers Kygo , Röyksopp and Alan Walker , to indie artists Girl In Red , Aurora , Kings of Convenience , and the legendary new wave act a-ha .

With Bergtatt Festival , presented in Luster, Western Norway, on an epic fjord, the Nordic country also boasts one of Europe’s most specular and remote festivals, with a killer, curated lineup.

Billboard’s Lars Brandle made the journey for the 2026 edition, hosted on the first weekend of July, and discovered an event like no other, a musical wonderland powered by a small army of volunteers, all of it playing out in a spot that could be lifted right out the mind of Tolkien.

Bergtatt Festival 2026 opening concert at the Berge.

Aksel Xavier Rustad

A holiday in paradise

The Norwegian summer isn’t like currency. You can’t bank it. In a place like Luster, a municipality and village in Vestland county on the inner, eastern end of the Sognefjorden, Europe’s longest fjord, the four seasons can make their appearance before breakfast. No biggie. After those long, cold winters, summer in this part of the world is a reward. It’s earned, a coming out party where everyone is invited.

Presented several days after the summer solstice, Bergtatt Festival 2026 invites all those elements. Snowcapped mountains nearby, and days so long a mind can be tricked into considering dinner plans well past midnight. This party, a camping fest, welcomes about 1,500 guests, including 1,000 ticket-buyers, the rest comprised of friends, family and guests.

It’s a swift sellout.

Founded in 2018, and opening its gates for the first time in 2019, Bergtatt is led by six school friends from Oslo: Oskar Skulberg (booking manager), Anders Mageli (community leader), Nicolai Frantzen (creative leader), Johan Stang (operational leader), Ole Kristian Knudsen (technical leader) and Aksel Mjøen (commercial leader). The seed was planted on a trip to visit the Mageli cabin, the lads sampling some wine.

Today, the event boasts some 30 core, unpaid volunteers. That number grows to about 150 for showtime. And like the co-founders, each helper has their own, specific role to play. Most of that initial launch crew, numbering 10 to 20, remain part of the team.

Each of the founders has a “normal jobs, which I think gives a certain perspective,” remarks Stang. Bergtatt “is our hobby.”

Bergtatt is different. “Our booking budget is proportionately way too high compared to what’s normal,” Skulberg reckons, “because we do it for fun.” This year, 30 acts and 30 events are booked.

As the fest has matured, it has remained right-sized. Like every other live event on earth, the pandemic did its damage. Two editions were wiped out, and co-founder Mathias Apeland exited to pursue other ventures. The festival survived and thrived, where so many others have imploded under the weight of costs and changing ticket-buying behaviors. It’s a feast for the eyes and ears, a music holiday with a roadtrip.

Camoufly performs in Bergheim at Norway’s Bergtatt Festival 2026.

Stian Werme

An early vision was to present the fest on the peak of the Berge mountain, where the family of co-founder Mageli has a property. That logistical nightmare was tamed, sanity prevailed, and the show is now presented at ground level.

The mountain plays its part. The fest gets underway only after a mass hike to the summit, followed by the “Berge Uphill Race,” contested by folks considerably fitter than the rest of us. And then, a performance, this time featuring a stripped-back set by Konradsen . Mother nature flexing in the background. “The most important thing is community and music,” Mageli remarks at the mic. On the walk down, a dance party pumps away in the forest, and presents an opportunity for hundreds to stretch the legs.

Music festivals need an angle. Money is tight, time is money. The United States’ Burning Man is a rite of passage, and owns its place on the calendar. Australia’s Big Red Bash is held in the desert. Others set up on islands, alps, with a-list lineups. 

With Bergtatt Festival, the journey is intrinsic to the experience. From Oslo, the capital, 220 miles to the south, the journey cuts through ranges and includes at least one section by ferry. It’s grand scenery, where mountainous woodland meets glacier water, a wilderness that belongs in Middle Earth.

From Bergen, the country’s second city, a drive passes through the Lærdal Tunnel, at 15.2 miles the longest of its kind on earth. Add to that water paths, and there’s a sense of adventure before the action starts. You know it’s something special when the party-goers take snaps, which they do.

The trip, remarks Frantzen, “it tends to be a great filter.”

Linni Vibes performs at Norway’s Bergtatt Festival 2026.

Living the dream

For the lineup of performers, which included the U.K.’s Tourist ; local singer, songwriter and bandleader Fay Wildhagen ; enigmatic soulman Pale Jay ; Keisha , a large-lunged Swedish artist who blew open the door on her career by posting songs on TikTok; and pianist, composer and electronic artist Vetle Nærø , who performed in the Dale Church, established around 1220-1250 (a “very special event,” he later says), Bergtatt is an eye-opener.

“It’s a dream here, in such a wonderful location, and an incredible sound system,” remarks Faux Tales , the electronic music producer from Bern, Switzerland, during his day three set in the Bergheim room, a 100-year-old cow barn on any other week. “Enjoy that beautiful festival,” he remarks.

Several of the performers took multiple flights to get here. The members of Konradsen sailed. No one gets to Luster without putting in the work.

Once inside the gates, it’s fresh air. A pop-up tattoo desk offers keepsakes of the festival. Elk burgers are on the menu. To the side of the main stage is a sauna. And yes, the hardy locals swim in the chilly fjord as the bands rock out.

The festival counts a string of sponsors, but doesn’t rely on government handouts.

“It’s one of these things that I’ve always wanted to do, but has never fit the schedule,” Wildhagen tells Billboard . The beloved local artist and her band was meant to stay off the road this year to complete work on a new album. When she received the invite to perform, “I was like, ‘we have to come.’” With her day one headline performance, Wildhagen closed the chapter that is her award-winning 2024 album Let’s Keep It In The Family (via Warner Music Norway). “It’s been a dream to come here for many years.”

Bergtatt Festival 2026

David Barranco
@bjorkellingsbo

What the future holds

The 10-year anniversary of Bergtatt is on the horizon. Before that, there’s another event to plan for. A wishlist has been drawn up the headliners. It’s a work in progress. “We set ourselves some goals for the next year,” explains Skulberg, “and then we measure it after that. It’s in our mindset to just look for improvements all the time. We try to focus on the next year, every time. But we want to continue peaking or improving,” for “a much better product and experience.”

After the tents are packed away, and the site cleared, the team reaches out to ticket-buyers for feedback. The team doesn’t tune into the crowd when it comes to the content. That’s all done in-house.

“We can never compete with big festivals on headliners,” notes Frantzen. That said, the top end of town can’t compete with a holiday in paradise .

Expect the next show to be better, maybe bigger.
